extracted.subtask_short: PTAB IPR institution and evidence standards
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary/practice guidance for instituting and defending inter partes review proceedings before the PTAB, including prior art/printed-publication proof, timing (one-year bar), real-party-in-interest, common-sense obviousness, and motions to amend.  Aimed at practitioners preparing or opposing IPR petitions and amended claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 325(d) discretion — same or substantially same art/arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: "[W]hether the petition presents to the Office the same or substantially the same art previously presented to the Office," or "whether the petition presents to the Office the same or substantially the same arguments previously presented to the Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part framework: (1) Determine whether petition presents the same/substantially same art or arguments as presented during prosecution; (2) If so, deny review unless the petitioner shows the Office erred "in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims." Examples of material error include misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of relevant prior art impacting patentability or an error of law (e.g., misconstruing a claim term) where the construction impacts patentability. (Cases: Advanced Bionics; Puma; Oticon.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Material error standard for overcoming § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must show that the examiner materially erred "in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of relevant prior art that impact patentability; an error of law such as misconstruing a claim term where the construction impacts patentability. If petitioner fails to explain "how or why the Examiner erred," denial is appropriate (see Puma).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year statutory bar under § 315(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR "may not be instituted if the petition ... is filed more than 1 year after the date on which the petitioner, real party in interest, or privy of the petitioner is served with a complaint alleging infringement of the patent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must file before the one-year anniversary of service of the infringement complaint. The Supreme Court in Thryv held that PTAB determinations applying § 315(b)'s time limit are integral to institution and thus are final and nonappealable under § 314(d), meaning courts generally cannot review PTAB time-bar institution rulings on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections under 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(c) are limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 42.104(c) permits motions to correct "clerical or typographical mistake in the petition" without losing the petition's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 42.104(c) does not permit curing the absence of a timely-filed petition. If no petition was timely filed (e.g., wrong document uploaded so no petition exists on the record), the PTAB may deny restoring the original filing date because there is no mistake "in the petition." Compare ABB v. ROY-G-BIV (where a wrong petition was filed within the timeframe) to Varian Medical Sys. v. Best Medical (where no timely petition was filed because a wrong document was uploaded). Best practice: avoid last-day filings and verify the uploaded documents on PTAB's website before the one-year bar expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for printed publication in IPRs versus examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden/standard to establish that a reference is a printed publication differs between IPR proceedings and USPTO examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In IPRs, the petitioner must present evidence/arguments to make a "threshold showing" of a reference's public availability (sufficient to rely on it as prior art). In examination, the examiner need only make a prima facie case that a reference is prior art, invoking a burden-shifting framework that may require the applicant to rebut. (See Ex parte Grillo-López: examiner established prima facie case via public notice of hearing, presence of interested public, and law requiring transcripts to be made public.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence sufficient to show a thesis is a printed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony from a thesis advisor regarding university practice and deposit/indexing of a dissertation can establish public availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct testimony that the thesis was deposited in the university library, indexed, and available for public retrieval can satisfy the petitioner's threshold showing in an IPR (Seabery). Rely on witnesses with firsthand knowledge of institutional practices for indexing/making works available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions in other proceedings often insufficient to prove public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint statement of facts or stipulation in district court that a reference is a 'printed publication' may not demonstrate public availability for PTAB threshold showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB may discount stipulations made in other forums as possibly offered for convenience or other case-specific reasons. Best practice: supplement any admissions with independent evidence of public availability that can reasonably be gathered (e.g., library records, indexing, witness testimony). (See Argentum Pharms. decision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Webpage/date-stamp evidence alone is insufficient to prove publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: A date associated with a conference paper on a social networking site (e.g., ResearchGate listing 'Conference Paper – September 2012 with 45 Reads') is insufficient to show when the paper became publicly accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must provide corroborating evidence explaining what the date represents (submission, acceptance, publication, or posting) and more specific publication timing (day/month). Copyright year alone does not establish a specific publication date. A mere printout with a date stamp generally won't satisfy the PTAB's threshold showing of public availability (see In-Depth Geophysical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of uploading incorrect document on filing deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: If counsel uploads the wrong document (e.g., a power of attorney) instead of the petition and no petition is filed before the one-year bar, the petition may be found time barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB may deny a motion to correct under Rule 42.104(c) when the error does not constitute a clerical/typographical mistake "in the petition" because no petition existed on that date. Counsel should avoid last-minute filings and immediately confirm on the PTAB website that the correct documents were uploaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-party-in-interest identification requirement (§ 312(a)(2), § 322(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for IPR must identify all real parties in interest; failure to do so can result in denial or dismissal of the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit held that § 314(d) precludes appellate review of PTAB determinations relating to identification of real parties in interest—PTAB institution-stage decisions about real-party-in-interest are generally not reviewable. PTAB sometimes defers or addresses real-party-in-interest issues post-institution, and proposed rule changes may affect how testimonial evidence is weighed at institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense in obviousness (KSR/Perfect Web standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB (and courts) may rely on 'common sense' to fill gaps in the prior art when supported by reasoned analysis and evidentiary support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common-sense reasoning must be accompanied by reasoned explanation and, where appropriate, evidentiary support such as expert testimony. Repetition of an existing element (a missing limitation that is merely a repetition of another element) can permissibly be supplied by common sense under Perfect Web. PTAB's application of common sense should not be an unsupported assertion; cite precedent (KSR, Arendi, Perfect Web) and rely on substantial evidence (expert testimony) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 may be considered for proposed substitute/amended claims in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent owner files a motion to amend proposing substitute claims during an IPR, the PTAB may consider grounds of unpatentability (including § 101) that could not have been raised in the initial IPR petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory context: patent owner may propose substitute claims but they "may not enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter." The PTAB will evaluate patentability of new claims under § 101, § 112, etc., and issue a final written decision under § 318(a) "with respect to the patentability of ... any new claim added under [§ 316(d)]." Practitioners should expect § 101 challenges to be raised against motions to amend and should substantively respond to such arguments; failure to do so risks denial of the motion by preponderance of the evidence (see Uniloc v. Hulu). Also consider estoppel implications: § 315(e)(2) may bar grounds that were raised or reasonably could have been raised during the IPR from later being asserted in district court.
